# Tokenisation over Bounded Alphabets is Hard

> ICLR 2026. Finding a compression-optimal tokeniser is NP-complete and APX-hard already over binary alphabets, for both direct (vocabulary) and bottom-up (merge-sequence, BPE-style) tokenisation. Direct tokenisation stays strongly NP-complete even over a unary (single-symbol) alphabet. The intractability of tokenisation is therefore not an artifact of large alphabets.

Authors: Violeta Kastreva*, Philip Whittington*, Dennis Komm, Tiago Pimentel (*equal contribution). ETH Zürich and Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski".

Key facts:

- Objective: compressed length G_l(tok, D) = sum over strings c in D of |tok(c)|, the number of tokens left after tokenising the dataset D with a vocabulary budget of K tokens beyond the alphabet.
- Direct tokenisation: choose a vocabulary S (|S| = |Sigma| + K) applied optimally (shortest segmentation). Bottom-up tokenisation: choose K merges applied in order, as in BPE.
- Approximation ratio rho = (compressed length achieved by an algorithm) / (optimal compressed length), so rho >= 1 and rho = 1 is optimal.
- Binary alphabet: both variants are NP-complete and APX-hard (no PTAS unless P = NP). No polynomial-time algorithm achieves approximation ratio below 446213/446212 (about 1.000002) for direct, or below 7258949/7258948 (about 1.0000001) for bottom-up, unless P = NP. These constants are not optimised; the point is that no PTAS exists.
- Unary alphabet: direct tokenisation is strongly NP-complete (reduction from vertex cover). Corollary: choosing optimal coin denominations for a set of transactions is strongly NP-complete. Unary optimal pair encoding (OPE) is at least weakly NP-complete (reduction from addition chains). Unary bottom-up tokenisation is open.
- Hardness for an n-ary alphabet implies hardness for every larger alphabet (bytes, Unicode), so results for n = 1 and n = 2 are the strongest.
- Binary hardness uses reductions from 3-OCC-MAX2SAT (max-2-SAT where every variable occurs exactly three times), which is APX-hard (Berman and Karpinski, 1999).
- Open questions: whether binary tokenisation admits any constant-factor approximation (is it in APX), what compression efficient algorithms can guarantee, whether natural language makes instances easier, and the hardness of other objectives.
